FrMS88-e84800-d1e111.summary: Opens distinction 37, quaestio 1, asking whether God is everywhere (ubique). Gives the negative opening objection: since Isaiah says 'Celum mihi sedes est' ('Heaven is my seat'), God appears to be localized to heaven rather than present everywhere.
claims: Scripture (Isaiah) suggests God's seat is heaven specifically, which seems to deny that God is everywhere.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e129.summary: Gives the contrary position via the encoded quotation of Jeremiah 23:24 ('Caelum et terram ego impleo' — 'I fill heaven and earth'), then announces that four negative conclusions will be introduced to determine whether God is everywhere or only somewhere. States the first conclusion: God's being everywhere is not something fabricated by the intellect or an ens rationis, proved because no being of reason can be the real ground of something's really existing, yet God is really everywhere.
claims: Scripture (Jeremiah) affirms that God fills heaven and earth.
God's being everywhere is not merely a mental construct (ens rationis), since no being of reason can ground something's real existence, and God's ubiquity is real.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e155.summary: Gives a second proof of the first conclusion: whatever existed prior to any operation of the intellect cannot be caused by that operation; but God was everywhere before any intellect operated upon the concept, so his ubiquity cannot be a product of intellectual construction.
claims: God's ubiquity predates any act of created intellect and so cannot be produced by that intellect.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e162.summary: States the second conclusion: God's being everywhere does not denote something privative — i.e., it is not merely the negation of every place or the negation of distance from any place. Attributes to 'a certain modern doctor,' namely Peter Auriol, the view that God is said to be everywhere not through a respect of presentiality to the universe, in the way every creature is said to be somewhere through a respect of local situation (ubietas) to some part of the universe.
claims: God's being everywhere is not a mere privation (negation of place or of distance).
Peter Auriol holds that God's ubiquity is not a positive respect of presentiality to the universe, unlike a creature's local situatedness.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e179.summary: Argues against the privative account (and implicitly against Auriol's position): whatever has the formal ground of being everywhere would be formally and uniformly everywhere in the same way; but 'indistance' of the same kind that is in God is also found in nothing (nihilum), since negation of distance of the same positing applies to both — so nothingness would be everywhere just as God is, an unacceptable consequence of treating ubiquity as mere negation.
claims: If ubiquity were merely negative indistance, then nothingness would equally have to be everywhere, which is absurd.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e190.summary: Continues the objection with a further parallel case: the universal (a common nature/universal concept) is just as indistant from any place as God is, and yet it is not said to be everywhere — showing that mere indistance from place is not sufficient for genuine ubiquity.
claims: A universal is indistant from every place yet is not everywhere, showing indistance alone does not entail ubiquity.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e197.summary: Adds two more objections against the privative account: beings existing merely in objective potency do not distance from place, yet they are not said to be everywhere either; and every negative account must resolve into an affirmative one — the negative 'indistance' must resolve into the affirmative claim that God is somewhere (alicubi), just as a creature is said to be somewhere because distance is denied of it, so God is somewhere because distance is denied of him.
claims: Beings in objective potency lack distance from place but are not everywhere, further undermining the privative account.
Every negative predication must resolve into an affirmative one; applied to ubiquity, the negation of distance resolves into the positive claim that God is somewhere.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e210.summary: States the third conclusion: God's being everywhere does not denote something absolute but a relative (respectiva) predicate. Proved because whatever is in its formal nature 'toward another' (ad aliud) is not absolute but relative, and being everywhere is of this kind.
claims: God's ubiquity is a relative, not an absolute, predicate.
Whatever is formally 'toward another' is relative, and being everywhere fits this description.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e219.summary: Gives a second proof of the third conclusion: being everywhere is a predicate that applies to God contingently, from (in) time (ex tempore) rather than necessarily and eternally, and therefore it must be relative rather than absolute.
claims: God's ubiquity is a predicate acquired in time (contingent), which confirms it is relative rather than absolute.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e226.summary: States the fourth conclusion: God's being everywhere does not denote anything formally in God. Proved because God's being everywhere is not eternal, whereas whatever is formally in God is eternal; and it has already been shown to be relative, but God has no real formal relation ad extra (toward what is outside himself).
claims: God's ubiquity is not eternal, while whatever is formally in God is eternal, so ubiquity cannot be formally in God.
God has no real formal relation toward creatures (ad extra), which reinforces that ubiquity is not formally in God.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e238.summary: Gives the author's own affirmative conclusion, resolving the four negative conclusions: God's being everywhere denotes a respectus praesentialitatis (a respect of presentiality) that is formally located in the creature with respect to God — analogous to how God is said to act and create really, but the corresponding relational term (respectus) of that action is formally in the creature. Likewise, God is said to be everywhere by this respect of presentiality that is in the creature.
claims: God's ubiquity denotes a respectus praesentialitatis whose formal subject is the creature, not God, paralleling how relations of divine causation are formally grounded in the creature.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e249.summary: Raises the first of several remaining difficulties: is this respect of presentiality the same as the respect of dependence of the creature on God? The author denies this, distinguishing the question of whether God is the cause of things from the question of whether God is present to all things — one can be certain God is the cause of things while still doubting whether God is everywhere.
claims: The respect of presentiality is distinct from the respect of causal dependence.
One can affirm God's causality of things while doubting God's ubiquity, showing the two questions are logically separable.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e262.summary: Offers an analogy to explain how God is present everywhere: just as the soul is imagined to be whole in the whole body and whole in each part of it, so in its own way God is imagined to be present in every place by the presence that is (formally) in the creature.
claims: The soul's being whole in the whole and whole in each part offers an analogy for how God is present in every place through a presence formally located in the creature.
concepts: totus in toto, totus in qualibet parte

FrMS88-e84800-d1e271.summary: Raises the second difficulty: whether this respect of presentiality is a transcendens (a transcendental relation, i.e., really identical with its foundation rather than a distinct accident). Notes that some think every respect of creature to God is transcendens because such a respect is really identical with its foundation, but flags that this may not be true, to be addressed elsewhere, and defers the question of whether God's being everywhere is even true, pending the prior supposition.
claims: Some hold that every creature-to-God respect is transcendens (identical with its foundation), but the author signals doubt about this, reserving fuller treatment for elsewhere.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e287.summary: Turns to proving that God is in fact everywhere, grounding this first in Scripture (Psalm 138: 'If I ascend into heaven, thou art there; if I descend into hell, thou art present'). Raises the question of how this can be proved or persuaded philosophically, and introduces the first of several 'ways' (viae) used by various authors: the via immensitatis, according to which God, just as he is intensively infinite, is also extensively infinite — not by having part outside part, but by being able to coexist with infinite places — supported by the principle that the more perfect a spiritual substance is, the greater the place with which it can coexist, and since God is of infinite perfection, he can coexist with infinite place.
claims: Scripture (Psalm 138) attests that God is present in heaven and in hell.

The via immensitatis argues that God's extensive infinity (ability to coexist with infinite places) parallels his intensive infinity, grounded in the principle that greater perfection in a spiritual substance permits coexistence with a greater place.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e313.summary: Confirms the via immensitatis by analogy with divine eternity: just as divine eternity is infinite intensively, so it is infinite extensively, such that it necessarily coexists with every time.
claims: Divine eternity's extensive infinity (coexistence with all time) supports, by analogy, the extensive infinity of divine presence in place.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e321.summary: Rejects the via immensitatis as inconclusive because it proceeds from a merely credited (unproven) premise — namely, that a more perfect angel can coexist with a greater place. Offers an alternative argument along the same line: every limitation implies imperfection (as does finitude); but if God were somewhere and not everywhere, he would be locally limited like a creature, just as being able to exist at one time but not another would be a limitation with respect to duration.
claims: The via immensitatis rests on an unproven, merely credited premise about angelic perfection and place.
If God were not everywhere, he would be subject to local limitation, an imperfection analogous to temporal limitation.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e341.summary: Gives a second argument for divine ubiquity along Anselmian lines: God is that than which nothing greater can be thought; if he were confined to some part of the universe, something greater (existing in the whole universe) could be thought, which is impossible. Notes, however, that if these ways/arguments were sound, they would prove too much — that God is necessarily in infinite places, greater even than the whole universe, and that there would be infinite places greater than the universe, all of which are unacceptable. Concludes that God has intensive infinity but not the extensive infinity or magnitude these arguments imagine, so they fail to prove their conclusion.
claims: The Anselmian 'nothing greater can be thought' argument would require God not be confined to any part of the universe.
If sound, the immensitatis-style arguments would entail unacceptable consequences (infinite places greater than the universe), so they are rejected.
God possesses intensive infinity but not the kind of extensive infinity these arguments presuppose.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e365.summary: Introduces the second via used by some authors: the via causalitatis. It requires that an agent be present and approximate to the patient it acts upon; but God acts everywhere; therefore God is everywhere.
claims: An agent must be present to the patient it acts on.
Since God acts everywhere, God must be present everywhere.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e372.summary: Rejects the via causalitatis as non-demonstrative, since it may rest on the merely credited premise that God acts immediately in the action of a natural agent — a premise some do not accept.
claims: The via causalitatis rests on the disputed, merely credited premise that God acts immediately within natural agency.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e379.summary: Gives a further argument against the requirement that an agent be locally present to its patient: the stronger an agent is, the more it can act at a distance; and we observe secondary agents acting where they are not present, as the sun acts in the depths of the earth.
claims: Stronger agents can act at greater distances.
The sun causes effects in the depths of the earth despite not being locally present there, showing agents can act without local presence.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e383.summary: Considers a third possible reply: granting that natural agents must be locally present, this is because they act through contact and so require approximation, whereas God does not act through such contact. Responds that the objection still does not convince, since natural agents themselves appear able to act where they are not present.
claims: Natural agents act by contact and thus require proximity, but God does not act by contact.
Even granting this, natural agents appear capable of acting where they are not locally present, undermining the requirement of local presence for agency in general.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e399.summary: Introduces a possible objection: perhaps such agents act 'in the medium' (in medio), i.e., through an intervening causal chain, rather than directly at a distance.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e403.summary: Rejects the 'action in the medium' explanation: it is certain that the sun's action in the depths of the earth is not exercised in the intervening medium, and it is false to say such action always occurs in the medium — an angel speaking to another causes nothing in the medium between them, whether of the same or a different kind as the effect at the terminus, so only virtual contact suffices for action.
claims: The sun does not act in the depths of the earth via an intervening medium.
An angel speaking to another causes no effect in the intervening medium.
Virtual (rather than physical/local) contact suffices for causal action.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e416.summary: Adds that the causal argument is insufficient to establish the intended conclusion in any case: if God were determinately located in heaven, he could still simply influence things below, just as the sun, though situated in its own orbit, influences things at a distance.
claims: Even a determinately located God (in heaven) could influence the lower world, as the sun does from its orbit, so the causal argument fails to prove full ubiquity.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e425.summary: Distinguishes two ways God's being everywhere could be posited. First, that God is in one determinate place of the universe and influences all things from there, as the sun does — a view some hold requires acting first in the medium and then at the terminus, like a philosophical agent whose power is sited somewhere; but this lacks plausibility since God does not act through corporeal influx but through will alone, reaching the extremes directly as will attains its object without intermediaries. Second, that God is abstracted from every place so as to be truly nowhere and consequently not everywhere, acting through indistance (since what is nowhere is distant from nothing, distance presupposing a 'where'); but this too is rejected, because one cannot infer from a consequent something that contradicts the antecedent — from not being anywhere, indistance follows, and from indistance, being everywhere follows, yet 'being everywhere' and 'not being anywhere' are themselves contradictory.
claims: One view: God is determinately located and influences all things from that location, like the sun — rejected because God acts through will alone, not corporeal influx, and so does not need to act first in a medium.

Another view: God is abstracted from all place ('nowhere') and acts through indistance — rejected because 'being everywhere' and 'not being anywhere' are logically contradictory, so this account cannot coherently ground ubiquity.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e462.summary: Introduces the third via used by some to prove divine ubiquity: the argument from immutability. If God were not everywhere, he could be moved from place to place by transferring himself from one part of the world to another, and so would be locally changed — for whatever could be in another place just as in this one is proved capable of such change, since when God created the world he could have determined for himself whichever part he willed, one part not repugning to him more than another, and so by the same reasoning he can now be in whatever does not repugn to him.
claims: If God were not everywhere, he could move from place to place and so undergo local change.
Since no part of the universe is more repugnant to God than another (as shown at creation), God can now be present wherever nothing repugns to him.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e482.summary: Adds a further argument: if God were determined to some one place such that he could not be presentially in another, this would seem to make him enclosed and would import imperfection — even though this very limitation is denied of angels on account of angelic freedom and dignity, and an angel is more determined to a place than God is, which would make God's supposed limitation even more incongruous.
claims: Being confined to one place would import imperfection in God.
Angels, though more determined to place than God, are by their dignity and freedom denied such confinement — a fortiori this confinement should not apply to God.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e495.summary: Rejects the immutability-based via as also inconclusive: one could say God is properly nowhere but transferably wherever he is, such that he would not be changed by this; and even granting that he is properly somewhere, it still would not follow that God changes, since the relation of the located to the place (the 'where') is not had by God but rather the place has a respect of presentiality to what is located. Thus God would be said to be transferred from place to place through a new respect of presentiality in the new place toward God — one that did not exist before — from which God is denominated to be in something he was not in before, just as was said earlier regarding new creation in the creature occurring without anything new in God. Even if God is posited as wholly abstracted from place ('nowhere'), the argument does not convince, because there is no local change where there is total abstraction from place; but if God is posited as determinately in heaven, as simple people imagine, the argument seems to proceed apparently but still does not convince — because just as God becomes creator from non-creator, and lord from non-lord, solely through a new respect of the creature toward him, so he could become present to something he was not present to before solely through a new respect of presentiality of the creature toward God, which the creature would receive, just as a mover impresses the 'where' itself upon the moved.
claims: The relation of location ('where') belongs formally to the place, not to God, so God's presence in a new place can be explained by a new relation arising in the creature, without change in God.

By analogy with God becoming creator or lord solely through a new relation in the creature (without change in God), God could become present somewhere new solely through a new respect of presentiality impressed on the creature.
concepts: new relation without change in God

FrMS88-e84800-d1e559.summary: Raises a further question arising from the preceding analysis: whether, by this same mode, one body could be transferred by divine power from one place to another through a mere change of relation of place, without anything else changing.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e570.summary: Answers the preceding question affirmatively: God could produce one relation without its opposite relation, and in that case the body would not be said to be moved or changed, even though its relation of place had altered.
claims: God could bring about one relation without the corresponding opposite relation, in which case a body's place could change without the body being properly moved or changed.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e577.summary: Introduces the fourth via, from coexistentia, attributed to an unnamed doctor: every creature has a necessary presentiality toward God, analogous to a coexistence of duration; and since God is somewhere, this occurs through the respect of presentiality of the creature toward him, and since every creature is necessarily present [to God], God will necessarily be everywhere.
claims: Every creature necessarily coexists with God in presentiality, analogous to durational coexistence.
Because every creature is necessarily present to God, God is necessarily everywhere.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e595.summary: Notes that since the necessity of this respect of coexistentia is not self-evident, it is confirmed by four further arguments; gives the first: if God, with the heavens destroyed, were to create a star, he could move it circularly, but only if it acquired some respect — and this could only be a respect of presentiality toward God himself.
claims: A hypothetically created star (with the heavens destroyed) could be moved circularly by God only by acquiring a relation, which must be one of presentiality toward God.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e608.summary: Gives the second confirming argument: if God destroyed the whole universe except the poles, he could join them and move them perpendicularly, but only through a respect of presentiality toward himself as the first (unmoved) term.
claims: A thought experiment involving the destruction of the universe except its poles shows that their motion would require a respect of presentiality toward God as the unmoved reference.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e619.summary: Gives the third confirming argument: God can move all things simultaneously, and this is possible only through some respect — not a respect of things to one another, but a respect to God.
claims: God's simultaneous movement of all things requires a respect, and this respect must be to God rather than among the things themselves.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e629.summary: Gives the fourth confirming argument: whatever is moved has a respect to something immobile; but that immobile term can only be God, and so all moved things have a respect to God.
claims: Whatever moves has a relation to something immobile, and that immobile term can only be God.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e636.summary: States that once the immobility of place — called the most difficult passage in all of philosophy — has been established, the point at issue becomes clear, but defers full treatment of that topic to book two (of the Sentences commentary).
claims: The immobility of place is the most difficult topic in philosophy; its resolution clarifies the present question but is deferred to book two.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e645.summary: Gives the author's final determinative conclusion to the whole quaestio: God is everywhere.
claims: God is everywhere.

FrMS88-e84800-d1e648.summary: Closes the quaestio by responding to the initial objection (that Isaiah's 'heaven is my seat' implies God is not everywhere), stating that the answer is already evident from what has been said.
claims: The opening objection from Isaiah is resolved by the preceding determination that God's ubiquity is a matter of relative presentiality grounded in creatures, not spatial confinement.

FrMS88-e84800.summary: Quaestio 1 of distinction 37 asks whether God is everywhere (ubique). It opens with the objection that Isaiah's 'heaven is my seat' implies God's presence is localized, against the contrary scriptural claim (Jeremiah 23:24, quoted directly) that God fills heaven and earth. The question is resolved through four negative conclusions — God's ubiquity is not an ens rationis, not a privation, not something absolute, and not formally in God — followed by the author's own affirmative determination that it denotes a respectus praesentialitatis formally grounded in the creature toward God, illustrated by the analogy of the soul being whole in the whole and in each part of the body. Two further difficulties are addressed: whether this respect is one of causal dependence (denied — presence and causality are distinct questions) and whether it is a transcendental relation (left open). The bulk of the quaestio then surveys and critically rejects four traditional 'ways' of proving that God is in fact everywhere — via immensitatis (extensive infinity, rejected as resting on an unproven premise about angelic perfection and as implying absurd infinities), via causalitatis (agent-patient presence, rejected because agents can act without local presence, e.g. the sun or an angel's speech, and because even a spatially confined God could still influence everything, like the sun), via immutabilitatis (avoiding local motion, addressed via the notion that a new presence can arise through a new relation in the creature without change in God, paralleled to God becoming creator or lord), and via coexistentiae (the necessary presentiality of every creature to God, confirmed by four thought experiments involving destruction and re-creation of parts of the universe and the question of a first unmoved term of motion). The full resolution of these arguments is said to depend on the immobility of place, 'the most difficult passage in all philosophy,' deferred to book two. The quaestio concludes with the bare determination that God is everywhere, and a brief resolution of the opening Isaiah-based objection.
claims: God is everywhere, but this ubiquity is a relative predicate (a respectus praesentialitatis) formally grounded in the creature, not an absolute or intrinsic determination of God.

None of the four traditional proof-strategies for divine ubiquity (immensitatis, causalitatis, immutabilitatis, coexistentiae) is fully demonstrative as commonly presented; each rests on contestable or merely credited premises.
God's presence to a new place, like his becoming creator or lord, can be explained through a new relation arising in the creature, without any real change in God himself.
The full philosophical resolution of divine ubiquity depends on the doctrine of the immobility of place, treated in book two.
